Hello,

There are no fixed fees for copyright infringements and the compensation always depends on the circumstances: what image(s) was used, how long the image was used, who is the copyright holder, who is the infringer, country of infringement (different countries have different case law). In practice I have seen claims between 1000 EUR - 170K EUR.  

Please also note that in addition to the damages claim, copyright holders always request removal of the photos. Thus, payment does not entitle the infringer to continue using the photos.

As a general rule, it is always cheaper to hire a photographer to make images of our own than use third party images without permission.

Best,

Indrek

	SELECT
		*
	FROM
		json_table(@citysource,
			'$[*]' columns (id int path '$.id',
				name varchar(100)
				path '$.name')) AS jt
),
leadrawdata AS (
	SELECT
		id,
		JSON_UNQUOTE(data_json -> "$.data.FMBaEKs7") full_name
	FROM
		lead_raw_data
	WHERE
		form_id = 25
		AND processing_status = 'invalid'
		AND link_token = ''

	SELECT
		id,
		full_name,
		first_name,
		last_name,
		email,
		phone,
		city_id,
		personal_unique_token,
		created
	FROM
		`lead`
	WHERE

		AND full_name in(

	ORDER BY

),

		id,
		full_name,
		first_name,
		last_name,
		email,
		personal_unique_token,
		phone,
		city_id
	FROM (
		SELECT
			*,
			ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY full_name ORDER BY id DESC) rn
		FROM
			leaddata) t
	WHERE
		rn = 1
),
updatesource AS (
SELECT
	lrd.*,
	ld.first_name,
	ld.last_name,
	ld.email,
	ld.phone,
	ld.personal_unique_token,
	cs.name AS city_name,

FROM
	leadrawdata lrd
	JOIN latestleaddata ld ON lrd.full_name = ld.full_name

)
SELECT
	*

So there are requests to [com.cn|http://com.cn] domains, which take a bunch of time, which affect the overall statistic which used by alerts, and the overall state of node-local-dns is quite okay. 

----

Also about difference with coredns, coredns setup what we have in fact, not working much as upstream dns server. 

And based on: [https://coredns.io/2017/06/08/how-queries-are-processed-in-coredns/|https://coredns.io/2017/06/08/how-queries-are-processed-in-coredns/|smart-link] , for all the requests it check k8s dns db, if no records here, it fallback to aws vpc resolver (/etc/resolv.conf). 

Meantime, node-local-dns handling all the queries by itself, what also brings a mess in comparing metrics of coredns and node-local. 

----

So what is the plan, comparing node-local-dns and coredns, the first one require more attention (based on pods DNS utilisation), but brings more wins in speed, caching, and mitigating conntrack issues. So the plan is to refactor a bit of labeling for metrics from node-local-dns, to split it from coredns, and highly adjust thresholds for alerts. And already during the maintenance, of the component, we may make some improvements in configuration if needs. (for example super long cache for such [com.cn|http://com.cn] zones or kinda).

*Hey* [~accountid:628b3e951a437e0070414307] / [~accountid:6012ab10dc29b4006a594649] / [~accountid:610279859798100070592384] 

We have now received the advice note from Burness Paull (‘BP’) regarding the ‘potential’ grounds for appealing the Nottingham Tender. 

{color:#006644}*In summary, BP has not yet found anything that would resemble a “silver bullet” with which to confidently attack the procurement outcome. However, there are several weaknesses in the process which give BP a basis upon which to engage with Nottingham City Council (‘NCC’), voice Bolt’s concerns, and seek further information before the contract is entered into.* {color}

+*Applicable regulations*+ 

The standstill letter referred to the Public Contract Regulations 2015 (‘PCRs’),  it is BP view that the council may have carried out the procurement process under the wrong regulation, however at this stage this point alone does not provide an effective ground of challenge (as the standstill letter has been withdrawn). Additionally, this is because the PCRs apply a stricter set of rules to the process than the concession contract regulations 2015. Therefore, BP's view is that it is likely a judge would likely think that by meeting the tougher PCRs standards, NCC also met the Concession Contract Regulations 2015 (‘CCRs’) standards. Even if they had used the CCRs, the result wouldn't have been different. There might also be a problem with the time limit for raising this issue, as it's been known for a while that the PCRs were used instead of the CCRs. Still, BP can mention this to question the overall credibility of the process.

+*Demonstration Day*+

Regarding the demonstration day, Bolt being last to present and the evaluators being confused at the proposal is not a ground for challenge. The demonstration day was on the 2 May, so even if it were, it is well beyond the 30 day time bar period under either the PCRs or the CCRs in which bidders can raise a complaint. This is also a subjective impression of the interaction with the NCC which may be difficult to evidence in court. 

+*Concession fee*+

During the call with BP Bolt discussed  that NCC had at one stage indicated that tenderers must commit to a concession fee/revenue share of a minimum of 7%, but that this was then changed. Bolt’s final tender offered a concession fee of 6%, but Bolt understands that DOTT (the successful tenderer) offered 7%, which will have affected Bolt’s price Score. Price was divided into three elements (guaranteed minimum payment, concession fee, user costs) – a maximum of 5 points was available for each. The best tender for each element (highest for GMP and concession fee, lowest for user costs) would be

awarded 5 points, and others would be awarded a proportionate score. Therefore, assuming that DOTT’s offer of 7% was the highest concession fee offered (it may not have been), then DOTT would have been awarded 5 points for this and Bolt would have been awarded 4.29. Given the overall gap in scoring (see comments on this below), this is unlikely to have been a significant factor overall in terms of the final scoring.

BP are not clear at what point (or where) 7% was stated as the minimum concession fee. A question in the clarification tracker dated 20 May says _“Given the weight the Authority is giving to Revenue Share by stating a minimum of 7%, can the_

_Authority please reconsider the amount of points that are being allocated to each of the commercial scoring criteria?”_ The response says _“Please accept our apologies, this was left in in error. A clean version should now be available in the portal.”_ So far we have not been able to identify where a minimum of 7% was ever stated. It is not stated in the invitation to tender or the invitation to submit final tender. Bolt’s initial bid offered a 5% concession fee, so clearly 7% wasn’t a minimum at that stage. BP considers this an important point to seek further information on from NCC as there may be an argument that it has engaged in a competitive dialogue process with bidders on different terms (e.g. emphasising 7% minimum to some and not others). This would potentially be a breach of the transparency, discrimination and equal treatment principles.

+*Voi clarifications*+ 

During the review BP found that on March 11, NCC might have shared some of Voi’s questions and answers with Bolt; some details were redacted in the spreadsheet. This could be a problem and a breach of Vois right for their information to be kept commercially sensitive. It’s possible that Bolt’s questions were also shared with others. BP raised this as something that BP could ask the NCC for clarification. However, this is speculative and it’s possible that Voi and other bidders knew and agreed that their information would be shared.

*General comment on scoring*

It's worth noting that the difference between Bolt’s final (weighted) score and DOTT’s was 13.73. That’s the equivalent of 80.76 quality points before weighting (or 16.15 points per the scores shown in the annex to the standstill letter). That is quite a significant difference. Realistically, any complaints about scoring are unlikely to move the dial very materially on this – it would be very difficult to persuade a judge that Bolt should have been awarded the contract (which is a much easier proposition when the scoring differential is small). There is, however, a question to be asked about the scoring _process_. Each quality criterion had a maximum of 50 points available (a total of 500 points). These scores were then divided by 5 (so each question is out of 10, the total is out of 100 – these are the scores shown in the annex to the standstill letter). This score is then weighted to reflect the 85/15 quality/price ratio (multiplied by 0.85). What is not entirely clear is how the 50 points are allocated for each quality criterion. The ITT gives a scoring table for scores of 1-5, not 1-50. It’s not that each criterion has ten questions (they all have different numbers of sub-questions, none of which have specific scores allocated to them). Nothing explains how they get from the scores of 1-5 (excellent, good, satisfactory, etc.) to scores out of 50 for each criterion. As the weighted scores (divided by 5) in the standstill letter are not round numbers (8.56, 7.84, etc.) this suggests that NCC has not simply allocated scores from 1-5 then multiplied and divided them, but has perhaps used some kind of moderation process or averaging methodology with multiple evaluators. As far as we can see, this methodology has not been disclosed anywhere in the procurement documents. We would recommend that we ask NCC for a detailed breakdown of how the scores in the standstill letter were arrived at. This element of the procurement has not been transparent, so there is potentially an argument that this undermines the reliability of the entire process.

*Scoring – E-Scooter Features And Capability*

John’s message also says that, at the demonstration day, NCC asked if Bolt could tender based on the “Dragon” (Bolt 6) scooter instead of the “Okai” (Bolt 5) scooter. Bolt did then tender based on the Dragon, and there was a comment in the originalACTIVE: 120380771v1 5 standstill letter which referred to Bolt being marked down because _“The BOLT scooter_ [the Dragon] _is largely new, and therefore has not been subjected to the iterative testing and improvements that other off-the-shelf scooters may have been subjected to.”_.

This could potentially be a breach of the principle of transparency – for NCC to encourage Bolt to change to a newer scooter and then to mark them down for the newness of the design. It would suggest that NCC had given inconsistent feedback, and had given Bolt the impression they would score one way before scoring another. However, nothing in the notes from the dialogue day suggests that NCC asked Bolt to change scooter. In fact, we note that Bolt’s written clarifications, shared with NCC on 3 May (the day after the dialogue day) respond to two questions about the Bolt 6. One question refers to the DfT approval for both the Bolt 5 and the Bolt 6 (which was ongoing at the time). The other asks about the lifespan of the Bolt 5 and the transition from Bolt 5 to Bolt 6. These questions seem to assume that the Bolt 5 would be used

(at least at first), rather than requesting that Bolt change their bid to use the Bolt 6.

*Scoring – Operations And Scheme Management – Battery Swap- Out*

John’s message also makes reference to the comment in the original standstill letter which says _“Could the battery swap-out schedule of potentially 20 hours from notification to swap-out render some batteries to be completely deplete if thereafter used 2-3 times per day for 12-15 minutes per ride.”_ John refers to the explanation Bolt gave at the demonstration day as to battery thresholds, priority alerts, fail-safe factors and how Bolt prioritises the battery as the most expensive component of the scooter. When scoring Bolt’s tender, the evaluators will have been assessing the tender document itself, rather than information which was discussed at the demonstration day. If the comment in the standstill letter is demonstrably not correct (and we can point to where in Bolt’s tender it is made clear batteries would not completely deplete in the circumstances described) then this could be a manifest error which would offer a clear ground of challenge. However, the impact that rectifying this error would make on Bolt’s overall score would be minimal. 

*Question:* [~accountid:628b3e951a437e0070414307] / [~accountid:6012ab10dc29b4006a594649] {color:#006644}*can you please identify if/where the tender demonstrates that this comment in the standstill letter is an error on the part of NCC?*{color}

*Scoring – Operations And Scheme Management – Parking Locations*

John’s message also refers to the comment in the original standstill letter which says _“The Authority was keen to identify how many parking locations (a location has more than one parking spot) and how many parking spots would be required to meet BOLTS needs, the moderation team felt that this question was only partially answered.”_ John explains that a great deal of effort was put into identifying parking locations, providing a map, and then setting out how future locations would be identified (via assessing user demand, etc.) The distinction here seems to be that NCC’s comment was with regard to the overall _number_ of parking locations, rather than the process for determining where parking locations would be. On that basis, we do not consider that this comment from NCC indicates a manifest error.

*Scoring – Minimising Adverse Impacts And Enforcement*

John’s message refers to the comment in the original standstill letter which says _“In this section there is also a commitment to address compliance issues within 60 minutes. While this is well received, the moderation team felt that realistically this could not be consistently achieved with the resource team being proposed.”_. John states that the BAFO was amended to include two-hour compliance on this.

However, the BAFO does commit to rectifying some compliance issues (such as an “Overcrowded Parking Hotspot”) in less than 60 minutes. It seems, therefore, that the comment in the original standstill letter may not be an error.

WITH citysource AS (
	SELECT
		*
	FROM
		json_table(@citysource,
			'$[*]' columns (id int path '$.id',
				name varchar(100)
				path '$.name')) AS jt
),
leadrawdata AS (
	SELECT
		id,
		JSON_UNQUOTE(data_json -> "$.data.FMBaEKs7") full_name
	FROM
		lead_raw_data
	WHERE
		form_id = 25
		AND processing_status = 'invalid'
		AND link_token = ''
),
leaddata AS (
	SELECT
		id,
		full_name,
		first_name,
		last_name,
		email,
		phone,
		city_id,
		personal_unique_token,
		created
	FROM
		`lead`
	WHERE
		city_id in(
			SELECT
				id FROM citysource)
		AND full_name in(
			SELECT
				full_name FROM leadrawdata)
	ORDER BY
		created DESC
),
latestleaddata AS (
	SELECT
		id,
		full_name,
		first_name,
		last_name,
		email,
		personal_unique_token,
		phone,
		city_id
	FROM (
		SELECT
			*,
			ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY full_name ORDER BY id DESC) rn
		FROM
			leaddata) t
	WHERE
		rn = 1
),
updatesource AS (
SELECT
	lrd.*,
	ld.first_name,
	ld.last_name,
	ld.email,
	ld.phone,
	ld.personal_unique_token,
	cs.name AS city_name,
	MD5(CONCAT(ld.phone,
	ld.email)) AS link_token
FROM
	leadrawdata lrd
	JOIN latestleaddata ld ON lrd.full_name = ld.full_name
	JOIN citysource cs ON ld.city_id = cs.id
)
UPDATE

*Overall, the Data Processing Agreement that IPQS included is not good.* It will not allow us:

* to comply with the GDPR standard when transferring the data to the supplier
* the internal standards for our data processors

*Details of the problems:*

* no clear timelines for the assistance with the data subject rights requests, regulatory inquiries and consultations, data breaches;
* no clear authorisation procedure for sub-processors;
* outdated international data transfer mechanism SCCs (Standard Contractual Clauses) - these must be updated with modern clauses. Such SCCs can be used as a valid mechanism for exchanging personal data between the parties.

*To summarise on the possible action points*:

* *Option 1:* update the DPA to our standard / provide our template for their review - to ensure more stringent privacy requirements pursuant to our internal standards  will likely take some more time;
* *Option 2*: update the SCCs - this will allow us to ensure basic GDPR compliance - but not all of our privacy standards. We should not receive any pushback on this, as valid SCCs is a legal requirements under the GDPR.

-Considering the urgency and the fact that the scope of personal data transfer is limited (IPs) - going forward with Option 2 should not create much risk for Bolt, but it ultimately is a business decision.-

Dear Виктор Беляшов

 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *02 July.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Conversation history* 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt

The Bolt Accessibility offerings include two key categories: Bolt Assist and Bolt WAVs.

Bolt Assist is aimed at riders who need additional help but don’t require wheelchair-accessible vehicles. This service features drivers specially trained to assist passengers with mobility challenges or cognitive impairments. Training for Bolt Assist drivers will focus on customer interaction, safe physical assistance, and emergency procedures, and will be co-developed with a reputable third-party disability group to ensure credibility and mitigate Bolt's liability. This partnership will provide certification for the drivers.

Bolt WAVs are equipped vehicles designed to accommodate wheelchair users, including ramps or lifts for easier access. Drivers of Bolt WAVs will undergo training on using these accessibility features, securing wheelchairs, and providing effective assistance. This training will ensure compliance with safety and accessibility standards, and the vehicles will be certified WAVs by the relevant council.

Both categories will operate using Private Hire Vehicles (PHVs) and will be integrated into the existing Bolt app, functioning similarly to other service categories. The offerings were approved by Gareth, Chris, and Emily. The planned launch is in Q4 2024, though we are currently behind schedule. {quote}* Starting balance for the beginning of the period
** This can be fetched from the 2nd tile called {{Provider Balance Snapshot}} column *Current Balance*
** Make sure you adjust the {{Balance Cutoff Date}} filter to fetch everything before the {{Created Date}} filter → then we summarise all balance entries (i.e. current balance) before the period we’re actually interested in. 
** For example by default we aggregate the main report monthly for the last complete month hence the default filter for {{Balance Cutoff Date}} is everything before 1 month ago
** If you want to aggregate it weekly then adjust the {{Balance Cutoff Date}} to everything before 1 week ago etc
** In this example the starting balance of this provider was 293.3735 gel which matches with numbers in Admin. For visibility we’ve also have the *Last Balance Entry Timestamp* column which will help you validate the results in this tile (it should be right before the period you’re interested in e.g. 31st May in this example as we’re interested in June data right)

* Positive impact on the balance:
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}

* Sales
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}
* agency fee reduction for campaigns
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}
* compensations
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}

** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}

* Agency fee
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}
* Cash pickups
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}
* Payouts
** Available in the 3rd tile called {{Provider Balance & Payouts}} in column *Total Payout*
** Note this is sum of weekly payouts (the actual $$ transferred over) within the period. And also includes the reversed payouts in case some payout failed on Monday 
* Total deductions
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}}

* Refunds
** Available in the first tile called {{Provider Sales Report}} if we’re talking about automatic refunds (Column *Refund Deduction*)
** Refunds via manual adjustments are in the bottom tile called {{Provider Adjustments per Subtype}}
* Tablet
** See below as it’s a manual adjustment
* Sim Card
** See below as it’s a manual adjustment
* Photo shoot
** See below as it’s a manual adjustment
* Campaign costs
** See below as it’s a manual adjustment
* other corrections
** As we have a bunch of different types of manual adjustments we can run for providers, both as deductions & compensations, we’ve agreed not to clutter the main (/top) report too much with it. Hence we have a separate 4th tile called {{Provider Adjustments per Subtype}} which will give users an overview of all different types of manual adjustments run within the period. They are included in the *Total Deductions* column on the top though (but doesn’t have the granularity) 

* Ending balance
** Ending balance can be calculated using the *Current Balance* from the 2nd tile ({{Provider Balance Snapshot}}) & adding the *Total Balance Sum* from the 3rd tile ({{Provider Balance & Payouts}})
** In this example the initial balance was 293.3735 gel & during June the total balance sum is 158.62 gel. There may be some small rounding errors due to difference in decimal handling between the Admin & this report but overall it should match.

Old product side documentation: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PDD/pages/2359853535/Rate+app+flow|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PDD/pages/2359853535/Rate+app+flow|smart-link] 

*General real flow*

Rate app is the [Modal|https://admin-panel.prelive.bolt.eu/modal/eaterModals/edit/483] and is triggering by the campaigns and should showing on start of the application.

On *Prelive* campaigns conditions are like Order Count > 100/200

On *Live* it’s more like Order Count > 1/3 depending on the country

Additional campaigns conditions are {{Not Seen More Than N Times}} (2) and {{Not Seen Modal Since}} (180)

*App level*

App is loading the {{/eater/modal}} on application start and showing the modal depending one type. Cause we’re requesting only one modal, not {{/eater/modals}}, if the user is part of multiple campaigns, we show only the one, returned from the endpoint. 

And it’s nor “dynamic“ type nor “rate_app“ type, nothing will be shown, like currently on *Prelive* with active “grouped_banner“ test [campaign|https://admin-panel.prelive.bolt.eu/modal/modalPollCampaigns/edit/2131278], and will stuck there until campaign will be active

*Possible improvements*

* To test Android (see the modal with our own eyes 👀 ) properly we need installed from Google Play app, so it’s *Live* env. Create the Test campaign without conditions except test users or actually have around 3 orders done and not seeing the campaign before
* Possible use {{/eater/modals}} in the app and think about the logic of showing modals one by one (Oleksii done tech preparations for that before for different reasons)
* [Debatable] Give client more freedom in when to trigger rate app modal. To not show it at the start of the app, but after the successful order, for example.

*Overall, the Data Processing Agreement that IPQS included is not good.* It will not allow us:

* to comply with the GDPR standard when transferring the data to the supplier
* the internal standards for our data processors

* no clear authorisation procedure for sub-processors;
* outdated international data transfer mechanism SCCs (Standard Contractual Clauses) - these must be updated with modern clauses. Such SCCs can be used as a valid mechanism for exchanging personal data between the parties.

*To summarise on the possible action points*:

* *Option 1:* update the DPA to our standard / provide our template for their review - to ensure more stringent privacy requirements pursuant to our internal standards will likely take some more time;
* *Option 2*: update the SCCs - this will allow us to ensure basic GDPR compliance - but not all of our privacy standards. We should not receive any pushback on this, as valid SCCs is a legal requirements under the GDPR.

-Considering the urgency and the fact that the scope of personal data transfer is limited (IPs) - going forward with Option 2 should not create much risk for Bolt, but it ultimately is a business decision.-*Update re my previous advice:*

Hi everyone!

I wanted to clarify our guidelines for deleting a driver’s account without needing a request from their fleet:

* Inactivity: We can delete a driver’s account if they’ve been inactive for more than seven days. This helps ensure they’ve been paid and don’t have any outstanding debts.
* Cash Payments: If a driver is set up for cash payments, it means there are no outstanding debts.
* Account Comments: The driver’s account should not have any notes indicating that it shouldn’t be deleted.

Should these criteria be met, the driver’s account can be deleted without obtaining permission from the fleet partner.

In our competitive fleet market, Fleet Owners have significant influence over the account deletion process, as fleet drivers are employees of the fleet and are provided with vehicles by the fleet. The Fleet Owner is ultimately responsible for deciding whether a driver should be released, as they were the original employer. Ideally, we’d prefer to receive deletion requests directly from Fleet Owners. However, if a driver tries to bypass paying debts by contacting us directly, we’ll need to reach out to the fleet.

When a fleet driver requests to delete their account, we need to check with the fleet to make sure they agree to the release. This ensures that any debts, fines, or damage issues are handled properly. Deleting fleet driver accounts without fleet approval could affect our relationships with fleets in a competitive market. Additionally, drivers with debts might create new accounts to keep working, which could lead to more issues for the fleets.

If a driver’s request for account deletion is denied, they are instructed to contact their fleet directly. This accelerates the resolution process and allows the driver to transition to another fleet or become a private driver more efficiently.

Given these considerations, we must carefully manage account deletions to support our fleets and maintain their trust in handling any issues related to drivers.

Currently, we have basic fraud rules in place for Early Cash-out in Thailand. For instance, if there is a high failed payment ratio or a suspiciously expensive order in the driver's history, either daily or since the last payout, we may prevent Early Cash-out. This doesn't mean the driver loses the money completely. Our rules are dynamic, and if the driver's order history improves, they may see the Early Cash-out button again, even the next day. In the worst-case scenario, drivers receive their earnings through regular payout.

If you find that this issue is affecting a significant number of drivers after this escalation, please let me know, and I will review the rules for Thailand further, as I did in this case.

_I understand it’s connected, but if a fleet driver wants to add a new vehicle, they primarily want to change their business type._ 

- Not exactly. In EE market, drivers are added to the fleet *only because they rent the vehicle and the vehicle exists in fleet’s car group*. In most cases, drivers have their own banking details (meaning they have driver based payouts while being under fleet). Only couple of fleets require fleet based payouts. So, when a driver is leaving fleet, the group in Admin he'/she’s assigned to changes, and we need to know the new vehicle details because if we don’t, we can not save the newly created profile (copy is done without attaching fleet's vehicle).

_In other words, what does the driver need to provide to the Beehive ticket so the OPS team can process the migration?_

* Driver needs to confirm that he has returned the vehicle to fleet and finished rental agreement. 
* Driver needs to submit photos of the vehicle he wants to use through the Beehive ticket and make sure that a vehicle card has been issued for this vehicle. 
* Driver needs to save all necessary data from existing profile, so when the copy is done - he/she wouldn’t miss any data after. 
* Driver needs to clarify which region he/she will be working in after he/she leaves fleet.
* Driver needs to confirm that his/hers banking details will stay the same. If not, he/she needs to provide new payout details. 

When necessary info is collected, a ticket needs to be assigned to Local Ops tier. We then can proceed with the process of copying the profile.

*Status update as at 1 August 2024*

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Current status*: waiting on new technical implementation details to update Employee Privacy Notice and conduct Privacy Assessments 
{panel}

* This Project has evolved over several months (from Q4 2023 → Q3 2024). 
* In January/February 2024 the Employee Privacy Notice was updated to reflect a new purpose for collecting WiFi connection logs to monitor ‘hybrid working trends’ on an aggregated level and a communication was sent out to all employees in Slack. 
* Bolt began collecting WiFi connection logs in Estonia, where the relevant hardware was installed and functioning. This has not happened in Poland and Romania to date, or anywhere else globally.
* In May 2024, following a request from Senior Management to access individual-level attendance data, Bolt went out to external counsel in Estonia, Poland and Romania to obtain legal advise on:
** _using WiFi signals / access card data that we've previously collected for the above purposes for a new purpose — understanding individual employee's attendance in the office;_
** _whether there are any restrictions around using employee attendance data for performance-management related decisions i.e. if the manager sees a correlation between poor attendance and poor performance? If so, what these are;_ 
** _other than updating the Employee Privacy Notice, what steps would Bolt need to take to ensure that these purposes of processing are lawful under applicable privacy laws;_
** _what level of communication to employees would be required to meet an appropriate level of transparency and notification;_ 
** _whether the fact that an employee is not attending at the office according to the existing Office vs Distance policy and existing employment agreement would be a valid legal basis for disciplinary sanctions? If yes, what would be proper disciplinary sanction to be applied for such violation? If not, what steps should be taken to make it happen?; and_
** _What is the process for applying disciplinary sanctions in each of the listed countries? What steps should be followed, what are the timelines and possible sanctions? Can employees appeal it, if yes, how?_
* Following the legal advise received, it was communicated to Senior Management and decisions were taken to:
** Make aggregated data available for the Management Team via the One Model dashboard. 
** Share individual data with MT members (whether this has been ongoing is not confirmed at this point in time).
* Action items across different teams (Privacy, Legal, People) were assigned. Privacy’s actions included further updates to the Employee Privacy Notice, conducting the relevant Privacy assessments (PPRA, LIA, DPIA) and reviewing any company communications about the monitoring — these are still in progress and will require updates due to changes in the technical solution being used (described below).
* In July 2024, the current method of tracking office attendance was deemed no longer possible. A new technical method will be implemented in the coming months. As a result, the Employee Privacy Notice will need to be updated accordingly, and these technicalities will need to be reflected properly in our Privacy Assessments.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Outcome of privacy / employment law research*
{panel}

{quote}As requested, the Privacy and Legal Team undertook research of privacy and employment laws to understand what is legally required to access and use existing individual (per-employee) office attendance data for performance management purposes. The research was limited to Estonia, Poland and Romania (priority markets).

# ﻿﻿﻿*Can the Management Team access the historical office attendance data collected up until now?*
Yes but recommend access is limited to view only for specific senior individuals (i.e.
Markus/Vincent/Kristi) and it must not be used for performance management or disciplinary purposes until steps below in (4) have been taken. |
# ﻿﻿﻿*Can Bolt take disciplinary action against employees based on historical office attendance data collected up until now?*
No - as we do not have the appropriate legal and people policies/processes in place to lawfully use that data.
# ﻿﻿﻿*Can Bolt take disciplinary action against employees based on office attendance data collected in the future?*
Yes - it is legally possible to collect, analyse and use individual (per-employee) data to take disciplinary action against employees who don't attend the office in line with Bolt's policies. However, Bolt can only lawfully use the data in this way once appropriate legal and people policies/procedures are put in place to lawfully use that data.

# *The following steps need to be taken to enable Bolt to do this going forward:*

* ﻿﻿The People Team finalise their Hybrid Working Policy (containing a description of Bolt's office attendance monitoring).
* ﻿﻿The People Team create internal guidance for managers on enforcing the Hybrid Working Policy (explaining how the data can be used by Managers, who has access, how to have conversations with direct reports, etc).
* ﻿﻿The Privacy Team update the Employee Privacy Notice to explain the intended processing and purpose.
* ﻿﻿The Privacy Team performs the necessary data protection assessments, so that Bolt can be in a position to defend itself if a Regulator comes knocking and to evidence that we have properly assessed the risks.
* ﻿﻿The Employment Legal Team together with People team updates the local internal work regulations in Estonia, Poland and Romania in line with external legal advise received.
* ﻿﻿The Employment Legal Team together with People team creates the local disciplinary guidelines (aligned to local Estonian, Polish and Romanian employment-law requirements).
* ﻿﻿The Management, People and Internal Communication Team prepare a company-wide communication to all employees about the new Hybrid Working Policy and the updates made to the Employee Privacy Notice to reflect new ways in which office attendance data will be used. The communication must be sent before the data can be accessed/used.

# *What are the risks if Bolt uses the historical office attendance data for performance management purposes before steps in (4) have been taken?*

* ﻿﻿Privacy risks:
** ﻿﻿High risk (90%) of reputation damage - if it becomes known that we used this data unlawfully.
** ﻿﻿High risk (90%) of large fine - the EU privacy regulators have a track record of issuing large fines to companies who unlawfully monitor employees in this way.
Notable fines include:
*** ﻿﻿France - Amazon - fined €32 million for excessive employee warehouse monitoring, breaching data minimization, transparency, and security standards.
*** ﻿﻿Germany - H&M - fined €35 million for excessive employee monitoring, including the collection of sensitive data.{quote}

{noformat}DROP TABLE glue.ng_public.cloudtrail_kewei1;

CREATE TABLE
    glue.ng_public.cloudtrail_kewei1 (
    event VARCHAR)
    WITH
        (
        external_location = 's3://cloudtrail-bucket-070511724387/AWSLogs/o-sjnj53dshq/451613234044/CloudTrail/eu-central-1/2024/05/20/',
--         external_location = 's3://cloudtrail-bucket-070511724387/AWSLogs/o-sjnj53dshq/451613234044/CloudTrail/eu-central-1/2024/04/',
        format = 'textfile');

SET SESSION resource_overcommit = true;

with event_records as (
    SELECT
        event_record,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.eventSource') as eventSource,
        parse_datetime(json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.eventTime'), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss''Z''') as eventTime,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.eventName') as eventName,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.userIdentity.accountId') as accountId,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName') as userName,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.errorCode') as errorCode,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.errorMessage') as errorMessage,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.requestParameters.databaseName') as databaseName,
        json_extract_scalar(event_record, '$.requestParameters.tableInput.name') as tableName
    FROM glue.ng_public.cloudtrail_kewei1 t(x)
             CROSS JOIN UNNEST (CAST(json_extract(x, '$.Records') AS ARRAY<JSON>)) u(event_record)
)
select
    cast(eventTime as date) as eventDate,
    errorCode,
    count(1) as cnt
from event_records

_Request the fleet (that is the employer):_

Hey [~accountid:641c083a67102fc717c1538e] there are no principal contractual nor transport regulatory concerns for this within markets where are live with Bolt Business.

Rather should be assessed whether and under which conditions it’s viable from the tax perspective.

And also by Commerce (Compliance) from the financial regulatory perspective. _If a User took a Business ride in country A then it did so under the country A’s Rides T&Cs contracting with say' Bolt Ops in country A for that particular ride. So based on country A’s T&Cs Bolt Ops is entitled to collect payment for this. If however say' Bolt Local Entity (providing Bolt Business and the single invoice feature in country B) is collecting fees for these Business rides happening in country A on behalf of Bolt Ops then that brings along the question - how can Bolt Ops as driver's commercial agent in country A use Bolt Local Entity in country B as it’s "sub-agent" for collecting country A drivers money._ 

Overall the single invoice/”resell” feature already within a single market [relies on diverging legal narratives|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1U48YL5wJm68RBrRMmKBSc15mMknSSidaptN_MHUuGtI/edit]. The cross-boarder element only complicates the matter further. So once we have firm insight also from the Tax and Commerce Compliance colleagues we can align and benchmark our conclusions also against the regulations of specific key target markets to be on the safe side.

Until then please consider it pending from the Legal end.

Cheers!

A.

I've been in conversations with Cassandra and working on a justification for this client fee to ensure we remain compliant with the commercial agent exemption under the PSD2 directive, and then I'll run this by Gerly for approval.

Additionally, I have integrated this fee into the global passenger fee project I am working on alongside Fernando Berzosa. The goal is to gather the various fees that the Ops teams would like to implement in their respective countries, find justifications for those fees to ensure compliance with the commercial agent exemption under the PSD2 directive, and seek Gerly's approval. This way, we can establish pre-approved categories of passenger fees that the Ops teams can easily implement in their countries without going through the entire approval process (legal, commerce, etc.). They will only need to consult with tax (to clarify the VAT applicable according to local regulations) and billing (to enable the correct and separate invoicing for such fees). After [conversation|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06R63EQ6CS/p1722432555740629] with Pawel, the following points have been determined:

* The account was created at 19th September 2019, whereas the current user claims to have created the account in December 2023.
* The ‘old user’ did not have login invalidated until CS logout. 
* The only authentication method was the phone (no social accounts were assigned to the account), thus the new user was able to log in only with phone number. He must have received it from the ‘old user’, and usually that takes place through phone recycling. 
* The mechanism preventing account takeover was not triggered since only it requires email verification after 6 months - in this case, the ‘old’ user logged in at 30 June 2023, and the ‘new’ user logged in at 21 December 2023. 
* According to Pawel, the phone number is now owned exclusively by ‘new’ user and there is no way for the old user to log in again. Additionally, in his opinion, no additional technical measures ought to be undertaken.

I can recommend two approaches for you:

* First is easy and requires you to regularly click “Save for later” when you work on big ASNs so that your work isn’t interrupted in the middle. Though time to fill out each ASN will be 2-4x longer, depending on the ASN size.

After that the ASN would be automatically created in a draft state which you can additionally edit if needed.

Based on the information provided to us, we understand that the request of the City of Imperia (“*City*”) has been made in the context of the following factual background:

# following a public tender launched by the City on 20.11.2023, Bolt Support Services S.r.l. (“*Bolt*”) was awarded the concession for the e-bikes and e-scooters sharing service (“*Contract*”);
# on 14-17.6.2024 Bolt and Distribuzione S.r.l. (“*3PL Provider*”) entered into two service agreements regarding some services that Bolt undertook to provide to the City under the Contract (i.e., maintenance, logistic and mechanic services);
# on 11.7.2024 Bolt informed the City via registered email that certain services provided by the Contract (“_logistics operations relating to the maintenance and commissioning of vehicles on the road_”) will be subcontracted to the 3PL Provider. This notice included 3 attachments, i.e. (i) a joint declaration on the subcontracted activities signed by Bolt and the 3PL Provider, (ii) an extract from the Chamber of Commerce regarding the 3PL Provider, and (iii) the certificate of the 3PL Provider’s compliance with obligations on social security and pensions contributions (so-called DURC);
# on 25.7.2024 the City replied to the above notice asking Bolt to submit – within 10 days – additional documents regarding the 3PL Provider and the relevant subcontract, pursuant to Articles 119 and 188 of Legislative Decree 36/2023 (the Italian Public Procurement Code, “*IPPC*”).

 

The request of the City appears legitimate for the following reasons.

* The subcontracted activities are expressly included in the scope of the Contract, which – based on the provisions of the tender specifications (_Capitolato Speciale_) – regards “_supply, distribution, maintenance and efficiency maintenance of 250 e-scooters and 75 e-bikes_” (“_fornitura, distribuzione, manutenzione e mantenimento in efficienza di un numero di 250 monopattini elettrici e 75 e-bike_”).
* Under Art. 119 IPPC (which according to Art. 188 IPPC applies also to service concessions such as the Contract), “_Subcontracting is the contract whereby the contractor entrusts a third party with the performance of part of the services or work covered by the contract, with the organisation of means and risks to be borne by the subcontractor_”. In the common practice, subcontracting is deemed to exist every time that the services to be provided to the contracting authority under a certain contract are partially performed by a third party provider also through manpower that is under the latter’s direction, supervision and responsibility. These preconditions seem to be fulfilled in the case at stake, where the 3PL is in charge for providing specific service through its own organisation.
* Under Art. 119, para. 3.d, IPPC, there is an exception for contracts of continuous collaboration regarding ancillary services, which are not to be deemed as subcontracts if entered into between the contractor and the third party provider prior to the launch of the public tender in question. However, this is not the case, here because the tender was launched in November 2023 and the service agreements with the 3PL Provider were executed in June 2024.
* The circumstance that the agreements in force between Bolt and the 3PL Provider do not shift to the latter the liability for the subcontracted activities vis-à-vis the City does not prevent the applicability of Art. 119 IPPC. As a rule the contractor and the subcontractor are jointly and severally liable _vis-à-vis_ the contracting authority for the proper execution of the contract, regardless of the different provisions, if any, which may be included in the agreements governing the internal relationship between them.
* The tender specifications (Art. 5 of the _Capitolato Speciale_) clearly state that “_The Contractor shall be required to perform the services envisaged on its own. Given the complexity of the concession and the importance of the services, any subcontracting of part of the service shall be permitted under the terms and conditions set forth in the combined provisions of Articles 119 and 188 IPPC, which are hereby referred to in full. The Contractor shall provide the Contracting Authority with all the documentation required by the aforementioned Article 119 IPPC in order for the Municipality to issue the relevant authorisation_”.
* The City was (correctly) informed of the subcontracting directly by Bolt and the 3PL Provider. *In this regard, we have no visibility on whether Bolt actually specified in its bid that the services in question would have been subcontracted. The City did not raise any objections in this regard, but you might want to double-check the bid in order to have the full picture*+*. Indeed in principle subcontracting is allowed provided that the services to be subcontracted were clearly indicated in the bid, and unauthorised subcontracting is a cause of termination for breach.*+

 

Please find attached the form that can be used to ask the authorisation for subcontracting (“_Modello di istanza di subappalto_” – see the first bullet point of the list included in the City’s letter of 25.7.2024), for which we understand you were not required by the City to use a specific template.

 

You will see that in the attached document we listed as annexes the forms that should be attached to the City’s letter of 25.7.2024, which however are not among the documents shared with us. We note that this list apparently refers most of these forms to Bolt as contractor (“_Ditta subappaltante_”) although in our view it would make sense to have them signed by the 3PL Provider as subcontractor (“_Ditta subappaltatrice_”). +*Hence we recommend that you double-check directly with the City if the reference to the contractor is a typo before preparing all the documentation*+*.*

Dear Armita Ghasabi 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *04 July 2024.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,

 

Bolt

Before I provide my support, I wanted to double check with Polish legal team.

*Preliminary position of the privacy team on the lawfulness of B2B sales activities:*

From the knowledge of the Polish privacy laws(Act on Providing Services by Electronic Means (PSEM) and the Telecommunications Act), our understanding is that hard opt-in is required in Poland for any kind of direct marketing/outbound sales activities. This stems from:

* *Article 10 of PSEM*: Prohibits sending unsolicited commercial information to individuals without their prior consent.
* *Article 172 of the Telecommunications Act*: Requires explicit consent for sending commercial messages by electronic means.

The fact that hard opt-in is required in Poland for B2B context was also confirmed by our external counsels from Fieldfisher.

Considering the above, it can be concluded that Bolt`s activities, although legal under the GDPR framework, are not in compliance with the local requirements. The sales activities conducted by our Bolt Business sales team do not rely on consent (as its practically impossible), but on legitimate interest (GDPR 6.1(f)).

*As such, I envision the response in the following way:* to generally clarify, that Bolt relies on its legitimate interest (GDPR/RODO 6.1(f)) to conduct its outbound sales activities and inform the potential corporate customers of Bolt about our services. Also, to clarify that Bolt provides an option to opt out, and undertakes to comply with the GDPR/RODO.

*Contradiction:*

However, I just found this [guidance|https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/index.html?t=electronic-marketing&c=PL] from DLA Piper - and it clarifies that for emails sent to general corporate addresses (e.g., [info@company.com|mailto:info@company.com]) and specific employee business emails (e.g., [name.surname@company.com|mailto:name.surname@company.com]), prior consent is generally not required. I could not find any corresponding clarifications in the Polish law/regulatory guidelines, unfortunately.

*Question to you:*

Perhaps in your practice you have already encountered such requests/questions issued in B2B context, and you can shed light on the topic? Is it possible to confirm that in B2B context, Bolt should not obtain opt-in consent?

Energy drinks that contain more than 150 mg of caffeine per liter as well as one or more stimulants like taurine and guarana are not allowed to be sold to minors.

*Lithuania, Law on advertising* [https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/dd69e1e2a58711e59010bea026bdb259?jfwid=|https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/dd69e1e2a58711e59010bea026bdb259?jfwid=|smart-link] 

Advertising of energy drinks is banned in educational institutions, concert or sports venues, theatres, cinemas, and in any media aimed at children.

*It shall be prohibited to indicate energy drinks as products of sponsors or advertise them in any other way:*

# in educational establishments attended by persons under the age of 18;
# at venues hosting concerts, sports, charity and/or sponsorship and other events for persons under the age of 18 and in advertising thereof;
# at venues hosting theatre performances, movie films and video films for persons under the age of 18 and in advertising thereof;
# in the media for persons under the age of 18 and in advertising thereof;
# in campaigns and contests for persons under the age of 18 and in advertising thereof.
# It shall be prohibited to distribute energy drinks free of charge for advertising purposes among persons under the age of 18.

Here is a more rigorous reasoning on why *IRR does not depend on the period*, for which we are planning spend.

# *Show that IRR does not change, if Cost and and GMV change proportionally.*

Below is the definition of NPV. IRR is the value of r (aka internal rate of return), at which NPV  = 0 (here we have 3 components, each representing a year) 

!npv_definition.png|width=538,height=113,alt="npv_definition.png"!

If we move from daily to, say, yearly, we proportionally increase both the Cost and the Revenues. 

This is the same as multiplying each component by some number _k._ 

!Screenshot 2024-08-02 at 16.49.30.png|width=594,height=68,alt="Screenshot 2024-08-02 at 16.49.30.png"!

But this means you can bring k out of the brackets:

!Screenshot 2024-08-02 at 16.49.33.png|width=594,height=68,alt="Screenshot 2024-08-02 at 16.49.33.png"!

A product is equal to 0 iff one of the multipliers are equal to 0. We know that _k_ is not 0.

Then, it means that for any _k_, IRR is same.

*Latex*

{noformat}\text{NPV} = 0 = \frac{k \cdot (\text{Cashflow}_1 - \text{Cost})}{(1 + r)^1} + \frac{k \cdot \text{Cashflow}_2}{(1 + r)^2} + \frac{k \cdot \text{Cashflow}_3}{(1 + r)^3}{noformat}

# Difference between two scenarios (two different levels of spend) grows proportionally to days for which you plan spend.

Hi [~accountid:5fc8dff0aca10c0069d470f1] - thanks for flagging. The template I have provided should be sufficient as an initial response in all cases where a rider has written to us complaining that a drriver has asked them for their phone number  4-digit code.

My thoughts on your Qs are as follows:

*_Are we supposed to leave these tickets on-hold? And what should we advise the user afterwards?_*

If a driver has complained to us about their own account being compromised, then the ticket should remain open until we can be sure that the hacker no longer has access, they have regained access to their account, and we have resolved any other outstanding issues that the driver has.

If a rider has complained to us about a driver’s account asking them for details that the rider finds suspicious, we should not be closing the ticket with the rider unless we are certain that the rider’s account has not itself become compromised as a result of the incident.

*_One of the main concerns that our users are raising is if they should delete their account, block their cards, etc. What can we advise regarding this?_*

* *Account deletion*: It is not for us to advise users whether they should delete their account. If the user wants to delete their account, they submit a deletion request to us and we action it.
* *Block their cards*: If the user that has complained to us about unrecognised payments from their account specifically, and we can confirm that unauthorised payments have been made from their account due to the actions of a fraudster, then we can advise them accordingly. I believe we have sent them the following wording in the past:

_“To the extent that there are any unrecognised payments being made through your Bolt account, we recommend that you do the following while we take steps to address your concerns:_

* _Please ask your family, friends or colleagues if they have recently ordered from your account using the same payment method._
* _If the payments are still unknown, please contact your bank immediately and block the card to prevent further unauthorised use. Please also let us know that you have done so.”_

*_Another thing the users want to know is what we’ll be doing with the user who is committing this fraud. What can we advise in those situations?_*

We usually respond to questions like this with standard high-level language, similar to the following, which can be tweaked according to the context:

_“The security of your information is very important to us, and we have implemented appropriate technical and organisational controls to protect your information against unauthorised use and against accidental loss, damage or destruction_. _To the extent that any unauthorised third party has gained access to your account, our specialist team will take appropriate steps to mitigate any adverse effects resulting from such access_.”

date(date_trunc('month',x.created)) AS month,
--x.payment_method_type,
--x.country_code,
CASE WHEN x.correction_ratio > 0.5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS correction_50, 
APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2) AS user_price_sum_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_ifp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.00/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),2),0) AS ratio_ifp,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_fp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.00/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),2),0) AS ratio_fp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS ifp_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.00/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2),0) AS ifp_sum_ratio,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS fp_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.00/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2),0) AS fp_sum_ratio,
ROUND(CAST((1 - SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_final_failed_payment OR x.uncovered_eur > 0 THEN x.uncovered_eur END)/SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_initial_failed_payment OR x.initial_failed_eur > 0 THEN x.initial_failed_eur END)) AS double),2) AS recovery_rate,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_chargeback THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_cb,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_chargeback THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.00/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),2),0) AS ratio_cb,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_chargeback THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS cb_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_chargeback THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.00/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2),0) AS cb_sum_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_payment_problem THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_pp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.is_payment_problem THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.00/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),2),0) AS ratio_pp,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_payment_problem THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS pp_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.is_payment_problem THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.00/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2),0) AS pp_sum_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.propagated_chargeback THEN x.id END,0.0041) AS count_propagated,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN x.propagated_chargeback THEN x.id END,0.0041)*1.00/APPROX_DISTINCT(x.id,0.0041) AS double),2),0) AS ratio_propagated,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.propagated_chargeback THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0) AS propagated_sum_eur,
COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN x.propagated_chargeback THEN x.card_captured_eur END) AS double),2),0)*1.00/SUM(x.user_price_eur) AS double),2),0) AS propagated_sum_ratio
FROM (
SELECT DISTINCT
co.id,
co.created,
co.order_id,
co.country_code,
COALESCE(tpr.price/co.eur_currency_rate,0) AS correction_eur,
ROUND(CAST(COALESCE(tpr.price/co.eur_currency_rate,0)*1.00/co.user_price_eur AS double),2) AS correction_ratio,
co.user_price_eur,
co.card_captured_amount/co.eur_currency_rate AS card_captured_eur,
co.uncovered_amount/co.eur_currency_rate AS uncovered_eur,
co.initial_failed_payment_amount/co.eur_currency_rate AS initial_failed_eur,
co.is_initial_failed_payment,
co.is_final_failed_payment,
co.is_chargeback,
co.is_payment_problem,
co.propagated_chargeback
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
JOIN ng_public.company_order_try ot ON ot.order_id = co.order_id AND ot.city_id = co.city_id 
LEFT JOIN ng_public.company_order_try_price_row tpr ON tpr.order_try_id = ot.id AND ot.city_id = tpr.city_id AND tpr."type" = 'correction' AND tpr.created_date >= date '2024-01-01'
WHERE co.created_date >= date '2024-01-01'
AND ot.created_date >= date '2024-01-01'
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND co.order_state = 'finished'
AND ot.state = 'finished'
) AS x
WHERE x.correction_ratio > 0.5
GROUP BY 1,2
ORDER BY 2,1 DESC{code}

More generally, my thoughts on Karolina’s proposal are as follows - *do you agree with this / have anything to add*, based on your experience?

* Collecting the driver’s name and email through the form:
** This is low risk, not excessive, and for a relatively clear purpose of enabling the driver to participate in the competition.
** The applicable legal basis here should be {color:#4c9aff}*consent*{color} - drivers are opting-in to the competition, and so should be opting-in to their personal data being used in this context. The Ops team should ensure there is a process in place for if a driver subsequently withdraws their consent.
** The main issue to address here is {color:#ff5630}*transparency*{color} - the current driver privacy notice does not cover this processing activity. As such, we should revise the wording in the form to include some transparency wording (and to explicitly address the collection of consent) - see draft wording below. We can then ensure that the master driver privacy notice is updated to include this type of processing.
* Processing the _driver’s data about completed trips / driver rating / number of friends invited_ to the platform:
** {color:#ff5630}*We need more clarity*{color} on exactly what types of personal data will be processed here. I would imagine this could be achieved by collecting only: (1) the total number of completed trips for August; (2) the average driver rating for August; and (3) an aggregated number of the driver’s friends successfully onboarded onto the platform for August - anything further could be excessive, and may involve higher-risk types of processing (e.g., processing the personal data of the driver’s friends).
** Again, I think the correct legal basis here should be consent, as only drivers that opt-in to the competition should have their data processed for this purpose.
** Again, the main issue is transparency - we can address this in the same way as proposed above.
* In terms of the revised transparency  consent wording to include in the form, I propose the following. This should be updated depending on the responses we get to our questions:
** “By providing your name and contact information, you hereby consent to Bolt processing such personal data for the purpose of registering your participation in this competition. You also consent to Bolt processing [{color:#36b37e}_information on your completed trips, your average driver rating, and the number of friends you have invited to the Bolt platform_{color}] for the purpose of calculating whether you successfully meet any of the conditions in this competition. But engineers usually use {{FireAndForget}} for Audit Log calls. This may lead to the loss of audit logs without any reason, and it will be expected behaviour.

Hi [~accountid:712020:7f0b3550-60c0-44c1-ab18-391c6e0b8688] and [~accountid:5cf539ddc756c10f35f28d01] ! 

I finally got the chance to collate local legal feedback for this initiative. Please find below my thoughts. In a nutshell, recommended solution is to give points on the sole completion rate and leave aside performance based metrics, which need to be greenlighted by the GM.



----

* Bolt Rewards is an incentive programme for drivers through which they can collect Bolt Points and *unlock low perks from third parties service/product providers.*



* From a legal perspective, Bolt Rewards has been reviewed by Product Legal and general legal advice has been given depending on the risk profile of the market. You can find the risk assessment [here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/19gQTYP1qwPrSi33ZZYcuryKGNxQ4oCd2JGMhW7_ohDY/edit].



+*Bolt Points metrics*+

* As you will see, general legal advice for Class 3 markets (from a reclassification risk standpoint) such as FR is to *avoid granting points on the basis of performance metrics and* +*consider only completion rate / number of finished rides*+ as being the only metric to gain points under the program. Despite the inherent level of risk of the program, linking Bolt Rewards with any performance feature already in place could significantly increase the risk of reclassification. 
* With respect to FR, we don’t have any specific criteria in the law banning access to these offers. However, under relevant case law facilitating access to work tools (such as fuel cards, electrification equipment) could *corroborate the economic dependence between Bolt and the Driver and be interpreted as evidence of the employment contractual relationship between Bolt and the Drivers.* Also, it could be argued in court that tiered offers encourage Drivers to drive more for/with Bolt to unlock better offers. Therefore, judges court argue the platform somehow influences the work schedule (as an employer would do) by pushing drivers to work almost exclusively for Bolt.  
* Considering performance metrics (such as the driver rating left by the passengers) implies conducting some performance monitoring and imposing sanctions (i.e. restricting access to offers) over Drivers. *Exercising powers of control and sanction pertain to employers’ prerogatives and thus it increases the risk that the driver could successfully claim reclassification.* 
* +*Based on the above, for the time being granting points based on the sole completion rate is ok as long as thresholds are realistic and do not translate into exclusivity engagements.*+  
* Should you +want to rely on performance metrics such as the driver rating, GM should assess the commercial benefit of it and take an informed decision based on the above, the associated ROI+ and having in mind that we should be able to roll the program back if backlashes. 



*Rewards* 

Considering the regulatory framework (and specifically Bolt’s obligations to provide upfront full details re the ride destination and Driver’s right to refuse orders) the only possible rewards to date are:

* Expedite CS 
* Low value tiered offers 

For low valued tiered offers, Drivers can be automatically opted in as long as they can unsubscribe whenever they want. 



*Contracts and T&Cs*

There’s finally no need of T&Cs to be accepted by Drivers to access the program and the Rewards.

We only need to negotiate some commercial arrangements with the partner providing the offer/service/product. To this extent, we can use the Bolt Offer contract templates and insert the specs and commercials of the tiered offer in the Annex 1. 



*Communications around the program* 

* As a general recommendation, please avoid reference to “loyalty” terminology in the local communications to drivers and app messages as we don’t want to give the false impression that this is an employee retention program. 
* In addition, please make sure that there’s no overlaps between Bolt Offers and Bot Rewards, specially when it comes to the communications to drivers.



Please let me know if you need additional clarification. 

Thanks, 

Michela

In Germany, all users are given Motor Liability Insurance (which is mandatory under German law), and users also get Personal Accident Insurance.However, this personal accident insurance will only respond if a user is hurt because of an accident and not a product defect. Under normal circumstances, we would have said sorry you fell off and sent them to the insurance company to be compensated. However, in this case, it appears someone has told the user that there was an issue with the scooter. This means our insurance will not respond as they will say the injuries were caused by our negligence.When we have had similar issues in other countries (i.e. no insurance in place), local legal has replied and explained that in our User T&Cs it says:

a)  You ride at your own risk,
and
b) It is your responsibility to make sure to conduct a safety check before riding.

However, I don’t know of German law and if this is a defence we can use. Also, considering a CS agent has said they can see an issue with the scooter, I am not sure how this impacts our argument.Therefore, this is not one for the insurance team, as it looks like we have no insurance to respond to these injuries. This looks like a case for legal to decide if we can defend ourselves and challenge it or make an Ex Gratia or without prejudice payment to the user.

Informing you that the start fee, per km fee, per minute fee are accurate and based on the [{color:#4c9aff}+*_official taxi rates_*+{color}|https://www.mcw.gov.cy/mcw/rtd/rtd.nsf/rtd71d_gr/278D51D51C13EA09C225777B0020BD0B/$file/Komistra%20%2025.7.22.pdf]. 

What is not legal:

* Cancellation fee
* Minimum price fee
* Fixed Routes Fees
* Surge

Are we operating the above? Yes, since August 2023 because we had no choice. It was either that or lose the market due to competing with non-compliant players plus inDrive which entered the market with their bidding pricing system.

This was a joint decision between the local team and [~accountid:60e96a31131bf80069e1459f] . It was also presented in this [+*_document_*+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1x07uJdPYOE4wmvKstx8ACMpPigLfkzSuOZIYAiI4-Ao/edit?usp=sharing] where additional parties were involved including from the Public Policy team.

The combined contribution from these under-the-radar initiatives to our GMV is 10+%. In absolute numbers, that estimates to €2+Μ for 2024.

The law in Cyprus clearly states that the rates are shown via two official government provided stickers within the licensed taxi vehicle. Furthermore, the only means of calculating the price is the taximeter. That said, no absolute prices can be provided neither any upfront pricing. The authorities had requested from us 2 or so years ago the fact that we were not showing a price range and as such we had switched to showing a price range. Nothing was said about showing the price components within our app as long as there is a price range provided but at the end of the day regardless of what the price range states, they declared via this [+*_announcement_*+|https://www.mcw.gov.cy/mcw/rtd/rtd.nsf/All/95C296435DF8973CC225898D002A89AA/$file/%CE%91%CE%9D%CE%91%CE%9A%CE%9F%CE%99%CE%9D%CE%A9%CE%A3%CE%97-%CE%9A%CF%8C%CE%BC%CE%B9%CF%83%CF%84%CF%81%CE%B1%20%CF%84%CE%B1%CE%BE%CE%B9%2010.4.2023.pdf][ |https://www.mcw.gov.cy/mcw/rtd/rtd.nsf/All/95C296435DF8973CC225898D002A89AA/$file/%CE%91%CE%9D%CE%91%CE%9A%CE%9F%CE%99%CE%9D%CE%A9%CE%A3%CE%97-%CE%9A%CF%8C%CE%BC%CE%B9%CF%83%CF%84%CF%81%CE%B1%20%CF%84%CE%B1%CE%BE%CE%B9%2010.4.2023.pdf]that the taximeter is the only means of calculating the price at the end of every trip and not before.

To this date, there is no law whatsoever that regulates platforms. All the laws evolving around the taxi industry regulates strictly on a driver level. In terms of price transparency, there is no price transparency in taxis since the law clearly states the taximeter as the only means of calculating that price. That said, all prices, even the final price of the app is indicative and as such the driver is liable to change the price according to the taximeter.

*That said, the fact that we are showing those specific price components while we are using all the abovementioned initiatives places us at an unnecessary regulatory risk should someone from the authorities or even a consumer takes a screenshot of the price components while they are surging. That comes in direct violation of the price rates since we are directly affecting and advertising them. By not showing the specific components since our pricing by law is ‘indicative’ that means that showing a price range as we are, even with surge, we are diminishing that risk and transferring the liability to the driver. At the end of the day, we need to protect ourselves as much as possible and always have that liability transferred one way or the other to the drivers.*

We cannot be 100% compliant since that would just shut our market given the fact that we are competing with non-compliant players and street-hailing where they are operating non licensed taxis and are not following the price rates at all. 

It is of utmost importance that we understand that these non competitive practices from the legal and illegal side of the transport market in Cyprus is affecting us and as such we need to bend the rules to our favor or be 100% compliant and lose drivers and growth to the other players.

These are the conditions of the market unless something dramatically changes and the authorities start implementing the rules and laws to everyone and totally by the book. This is not going to happen any time soon.

In the meantime, all our drivers can request price reviews for any ride. Price reviews that are below the app’s final price are accepted immediately but any price reviews above the app’s price are not while we have a procedure to be followed by the driver prior to approving the price review where we request a picture of the taximeter (if there is a deviation) and any luggage should it be related to them.
