** STATUS * (Updated)*

* *Estimated date / time of breach*: 30 July 2024 at approximately 22:18 (GMT).
* *Country*: Estonia
** NB. Unauthorised login comes from Nigeria. However, rider based in Estonia.
* *Date of Bolt’s awareness*: 5 August 2024
** NB. Bolt CS made aware on 31 July, when user wrote to Bolt claiming that their account had been hacked. User created a [new account|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/Users/user/226109836] in order to message Bolt about this.
** NB. Escalated to Info Sec team on 2 August.
* *Root cause*: It is unclear whether these were the actions of a hacker / malicious third party. However, this seems like a more likely explanation that recycled phone numbers, given that the unrecognised login was from a different country (i.e., Nigeria).
* *How Bolt became aware*: Privacy team notified by a Core Market Specialist team member
* *Nature of breach*: Confidentiality / integrity / availability
* *Description*: Estonian rider (Alexei Savoyard) received a notification that someone logged into their [account|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/users/user/132021761] from Nigeria. Estonian rider was subsequently unable to log into their account, as the phone number was changed. It appears that the ‘hacked’ account has since beed [deleted.|http://deleted.It]
* *Personal data involved*: If hacker gained access to rider’s account, they would have had access to any personal data visible on that account (including payment information), as well as the data on their delivery account. We also know that the third party changed the phone number on the account (we do not know if any other data was changed).
* *Number / type of data subjects*: 1
* *Adverse effects*: Loss of control
* *Aggravating factors*: Possible access by a malicious third party (although this remains unclear).
* *Mitigating factors*: The account at-issue has been deleted, and the user has created a new account in any event.
* *Remediation steps taken*: ‘Hacked’ account has been [deleted|https://admin.bolt.eu/user/users/user/132021761] by an OS agent. Appears that this was requested by someone - it is unclear whether this was requested by the genuine owner or by the hacker.
* *Severity*: Low. Subject to any additional information, I do not think this incident is reportable.

I researched the topic and can confirm that in the EU, consent would still be formally required for such server-side tracking, if it is not used for strictly necessary purposes, as outlined in my previous guidance for cookies.

This is because Art. 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive (ePD) would still apply. Server-side events, while processed on the server and not directly on the user's terminal equipment, still involve accessing information originating from the user's device and sending data back to the servers.

The law is aimed at covering any instances/technologies that track users’ terminal equipment, as they are part of the private sphere of the users.

After the investigation what I found is that on the 14th an increase was observed in response times. The same day the only thing that was “changed” has to do with 2 PRs that were released for {{delivery-eater-data-store}} 

* One done by Andrei Pit Rada ([here|http://unicorn-builder.internal/builder-ui/pipelines/216681?hide_finished_steps=1&hide_waiting_steps=1&refresh_interval=30])
** This change removes the usage of the caching layer for scheduled providers availability on the {{delivery-eater-data-store}} side in favour of fetching the schedule availability from {{delivery-scheduling}} service (where it is also cached in Redis). (as seen in the attached picture)
** *_This change can be blamed for the increase in response time we see since that day_*
* Another PR was released by me ([here|http://unicorn-builder.internal/builder-ui/pipelines/216558?hide_finished_steps=1&hide_waiting_steps=1&refresh_interval=30])
** This Pr consists of an improvement when fetching data from ES to only fetch the needed info from ES instead of the whole document info (here we start fetching only the provider id _vs_ fetching all the info)
** I’ve actually reverted this PR I released in order to understand if this had any impact on the performance and saw no difference hence concluding this change is not to blame for the added slowness. ([here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/105640] is the PR that reverts the changes)



Other mentions:

* I’ve also checked to see if there was any AB test started that day and there was none
* The event loop lag cannot be blamed for the slowness as it has not changed at all during those days 
* The number of requests made to all the other endpoints we expose has also not changed during those days where we see the increase in response times

PM 1 (6) Date 2018-10-23 Diarienr (åberokas) Polismyndigheten Rättsavdelningen GDPR - may you disclose personal data to the Swedish Police Authority? Summary The rules in the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) do not prevent private actors from disclosing personal data to the Swedish Police Authority's law enforcement activities. In some cases, there is a statutory obligation to disclose information that requires information to be disclosed to the Swedish Police Authority. In other cases, disclosure may be justified on the grounds that it is not incompatible with the collection purposes or that it is permitted after a balancing of interests. In such a balancing of interests, particular account must be taken of the fact that the Swedish Police Authority has a strong legitimate interest in the information in order to be able to fulfil its socially important and constitutionally regulated task of combating crime. Personal data shall normally be disclosed to the Police Authority without the data subject being informed of the disclosure. In some cases, disclosure may take place by ordinary email. However, if sensitive personal data or other privacy-sensitive information is involved, there is reason to consider other transmission methods that increase security but are also easy for the parties involved to handle. 1. Background The police authority's mission to combat crime is an important public interest. In order to fulfil this mission, the authority is often dependent on information held by private actors. This may include, for example, travel history from public transport companies, entry logs from housing companies or conversation history from community sites. On 25 May 2018, the EU General Data Protection Regulation became applicable in all Member States. The GDPR applies as Swedish law and replaces the Personal Data Act (1998:204). Certain general supplementary rules are contained in the Act (2018:218) with supplementary provisions to the EU General Data Protection Regulation, hereinafter referred to as the Data Protection Act. In many respects, the new regulations only build on previous regulations, but some things are new, such as the possibility for the Data Inspectorate to decide on administrative penalties when someone violates the rules. At the same time, many private operators have reviewed their personal data processing procedures. In some cases, this review has led to uncertainty as to whether data can be disclosed to the police's law enforcement activities to the same extent as before. 2 Legal Department 2018-10-23 2. Purpose and target group The purpose of this memorandum is to describe the Swedish Police Authority's view of the legal situation and provide guidance on how the police and private actors can cooperate on these issues. The memorandum is primarily aimed at lawyers who work with or come into contact with data protection issues within the Swedish Police Authority or in private organisations. 3. This responsibility includes ensuring that the authority has legal support both for requesting personal data and for processing it once it has been received by the authority. The police authority conducts preliminary investigations or assists prosecutors in preliminary investigations in accordance with the regulations in Chapter 23 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. During the preliminary investigation, evidence must be collected to determine who can reasonably be suspected of the offence and whether there are sufficient grounds for prosecution. In order to do this, the Police Authority often needs to access information held by other authorities and private actors. In the vast majority of cases, this does not pose a problem. In addition, if someone refuses to comply with the Police Authority, the Authority may, as a last resort, use coercive measures of criminal procedure such as search and seizure. The Police Authority has the right to process personal data for law enforcement purposes under the Crime Data Act (2018:1177) and the Police Data Act (2010:361). On 1 January 2019, the Police Data Act will be replaced by a new Act on the processing of personal data by the police within the scope of the Crime Data Act.1 The regulatory framework for the Police Authority's processing of personal data in law enforcement activities includes both preliminary investigations and intelligence activities. Data processed in preliminary investigations or intelligence activities is generally covered by confidentiality under the provisions of Chapter 18, sections 1 and 2 and Chapter 35, section 1 of the Freedom of Information and Secrecy Act (2009:400) (OSL). 4. This section summarises the parts of the GDPR that are most relevant to the issue at hand. 4.1 Responsibility for personal data It is important to clarify that private actors are responsible for their processing of personal data. This means that they have to decide for themselves the purposes for which personal data will be collected, the legal basis on which the processing can be supported and how long the data can be stored. It is also the controller who must ensure that individuals receive the right information about the processing and that the data is processed with an appropriate level of security. The Swedish Police Authority is the controller for its collection of personal data and the processing that subsequently takes place in the authority's activities. In a disclosure situation, the private actors must be able to rely on the Swedish Police Authority to ensure that the data is processed in accordance with the law. 2017/18:269. 3 The Legal Department 2018-10-23 only requests information when there is a specific and legitimate need for the information and a legal basis for processing by the authority. 4.2 Legal basis for processing personal data In order for personal data processing to be lawful, there must be a legal basis for the processing. The legal bases for processing personal data are set out in Article 6(1) of the GDPR. The processing of personal data by private parties is usually based on consent, agreement with the data subject or a balancing of interests (Article 6(1)(a), (b) or (f)). The DPA is clear that the balancing of interests can be used as a legal basis for disclosing personal data to a third party with a legitimate interest.2 In some cases, it may also be necessary for private actors to process personal data on the basis of a legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c)), e.g. to fulfil a statutory data protection obligation. However, in order to be able to invoke the legal basis of a task in the public interest or the exercise of official authority (Article 6(1)(e)), the task must be required by law or other statute, by collective agreement or by a decision made pursuant to law or other statute (Chapter 2, Section 2 of the Data Protection Act). Most private actors do not have such statutory tasks. 4.3 General principles, purposes, storage and the principle of finality Article 5 of the GDPR contains certain basic principles that apply to all personal data processing. These principles include that personal data may only be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes. This is sometimes referred to as the principle of finality. Another important principle is that personal data must not be stored for longer than is necessary for the purposes of the processing. Recital 50 of the GDPR makes it clear that there is no need for a separate legal basis for further processing of data, as long as the further processing is not incompatible with the purposes of collection. This means that data may be disclosed to a third party on the same legal basis used for collection (e.g. consent, contract or a balancing of interests), as long as it is not incompatible with the collection purposes. Article 6(4) of the GDPR sets out the circumstances to be taken into account in particular when assessing whether processing for new purposes is compatible with the collection purposes. These include the link between the collection purposes and the new purposes, the nature of the personal data and the existence of appropriate safeguards. In accordance with recital 50 of the GDPR, special consideration should also be given to the reasonable expectations of data subjects as to how their data will be used. 2 See information on [http://www.datainspektionen.se|http://www.datainspektionen.se|smart-link]  on balancing interests as a legal basis. 4 Legal Department 2018-10-23 The disclosure of material from camera surveillance is specifically regulated in Section 22 of the Camera Surveillance Act (2018:1200). In brief, the regulation means that individuals may disclose information obtained through camera surveillance to law enforcement authorities if the conditions in the confidentiality-breaking provision in Chapter 32, Section 3a of the OSL are met. This means that material from camera surveillance may be disclosed to, among others, the Police Authority if the information is needed to investigate an offence committed for which imprisonment is prescribed or to prevent, deter or detect criminal activity (e.g. intelligence activities) involving offences for which imprisonment is prescribed. According to the legislator, such disclosure shall always be considered compatible with the principle of finality.3 4.4. Individuals' right to information When personal data are collected from the data subject himself, Article 13 of the GDPR requires the controller to provide information on, inter alia, the purposes of the processing, the legal basis for the processing, the recipients to whom the data are disclosed, where applicable, and the storage period or the criteria used to determine this period. If the processing is based on a balancing of interests, information must also be provided on the legitimate interest of the controller or the third party. According to Chapter 5, Section 1, second paragraph of the Data Protection Act, the right to information in Articles 13-15 of the Data Protection Regulation does not apply to information that would have been confidential in relation to the data subject at an authority, which is often the case when the Police Authority requests information in law enforcement activities (cf. Chapter 18, Sections 1 and 2 of the OSL). Sections 1 and 2 of the OSL). 4.5 Security measures for personal data processing Article 5(1)(f) of the GDPR states that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage. Article 32(1) further states that the controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects. The starting point is that the higher the risk, the higher the security level requirements, but other factors such as available technology and costs also play a role. The rules on information security in the GDPR do not really involve any innovations and are similar to the previous regulation in the Personal Data Act. The Swedish Data Protection Authority usually recommends that sensitive personal data and other privacy-sensitive information should not be sent by ordinary, open e-mail. 5. Three different supports for disclosing data to the police In the light of what has been described above, there are at least three different supports in the General Data Protection Regulation for disclosing personal data to the police's law enforcement activities. 3 The bill En ny kameraövervakningslag (A new camera surveillance act), Bill 2012/13:115, pp. 104-116. 5 Legal Department 2018-10-23 5.1 Data must be disclosed if there is a specific data obligation In certain situations, there is a statutory data obligation that means that data must be disclosed to the Swedish Police Authority. In such cases, the processing is permitted because it is necessary for the fulfilment of a legal obligation. 5.2 Data may be disclosed if it is not incompatible with the collection purposes If there is no statutory data obligation, it should be assessed whether or not disclosure would be incompatible with the collection purposes. Indeed, as long as a disclosure is not incompatible with the collection purposes, the data can be disclosed on the basis of the legal basis used to collect the data, such as consent, contract or prior balancing of interests. When assessing whether or not a disclosure is incompatible with the collection purposes, the link between the original purposes and the police purposes should be taken into account. If, for example, the collection purposes are linked to the safety and security of individuals or to investigation and control, this indicates that the data may be disclosed to the police for law enforcement purposes. The confidentiality rules in Chapter 18, Sections 1 and 2 and Chapter 35, Section 1 of the OSL constitute an effective protective measure that must also be given special consideration in the assessment, as it prevents further dissemination of the data. In addition, as the reasonable expectations of data subjects should also be given special consideration, it should be emphasised that most people understand that the police may have access to data that is relevant to investigating suspected crime. 5.3 Data may be disclosed after a balancing of interests Processing, such as disclosure, may take place on the basis of Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR if it is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, unless the interests and fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject override those interests and require the protection of personal data. There is no doubt that the Police Authority has a very strong legitimate interest in processing personal data to fight crime. Therefore, even if there is no statutory obligation to disclose data or if disclosure to the police would be incompatible with the purposes of the collection, disclosure should, as a rule, be authorised after a balancing of interests in the individual case. This applies regardless of the legal basis used to collect the data. The police authority endeavours to be as transparent as possible when requesting information so that the other party understands why disclosure is important. However, given the nature of police activities and the strict confidentiality rules, the Police Authority is often not allowed to provide much, or in some cases any, information about the background to the request or the need for the information in the individual case. The preparatory works to the new Swedish data protection regulation state that all tasks that the Riksdag or the government has commissioned state authorities to perform are in the public interest. If the tasks were not in the public interest, the authorities would not have been required to carry them out.4 Although intelligence activities are in some respects not as regulated as, for example, criminal investigation activities, the authorities that conduct intelligence activities have also been assigned this task by statute.5 When balancing interests, it must therefore always be taken into account that the Police Authority's task of combating crime is a constitutionally regulated and important public interest. As stated above, it is the Police Authority's responsibility to only request information when there is a concrete need and legal prerequisites for processing by the authority. When balancing interests, the private actor can therefore always assume that the Police Authority has a strong legitimate interest in accessing the requested information, even if the authority cannot explain the background to the request in the individual case for reasons of confidentiality. When balancing interests, it should also be taken into account that the information is normally protected by the Police Authority through the confidentiality regulations in, inter alia, Chapter 18, sections 1 and 2 and Chapter 35, section 1 of the OSL. Against this background, a balance of interests in accordance with Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR must, as a rule, mean that a private actor may disclose information if it is requested in the police's law enforcement activities. 6. The data subject must not be informed of the disclosure It is often crucial to the Police Authority's mission that the authority can access data without the person concerned being aware of this. This applies regardless of whether the data is needed within the framework of an ongoing preliminary investigation or in the police's intelligence activities. Chapter 5, section 1, second paragraph of the Data Protection Act provides clear legal support for not informing the data subject that data has been disclosed to the police if it can be assumed that the purpose of the police measures risks being thwarted or future activities harmed (cf. Chapter 18, sections 1 and 2 of the OSL). 7. In what way may the data be disclosed? It is the data controller who is best placed to assess how privacy-sensitive the information is and how it can be disclosed to the Police Authority. It is also important that the controller ensures that the disclosure is actually made to the Swedish Police Authority and not to an unauthorised party. In some cases, the disclosure can be made by ordinary e-mail. However, if sensitive personal data or other privacy-sensitive information is involved, there is reason to consider other transfer methods that increase the protection of the data but are also easy for the parties involved to handle. 4 The Bill for a new Data Protection Act, Bill 2017/18:105, p. 56. 5 The Bill for a Crime Data Act, Bill 2017/18:232, p. 118.

T&C, transcrito) sem prejuízo da aplicação de outros critérios residuais de ordenação, observáveis em caso de necessidade de desempate, todos eles compatíveis com o RJTVDE.

a) os seis Participantes que, no final de cada semana, obtiveram o maior número de viagens concluídas nessa mesma semana na sua Região de Atividade (os «Vencedores Regionais»);
b) os nove Participantes que, no final de cada semana, obtiveram o maior número de viagens concluídas nessa mesma semana (os «Vencedores Semanais») a nível nacional.
(...)|

 

# Em suma, e de forma muito simples: caso o motorista violasse o RJTVDE, simultaneamente violaria os T&C, logo, naturalmente, seria automaticamente excluído da Campanha.

 

# Logo, são incompreensíveis as acusações, bem assim, porque especulativos e espetacularmente desgarrados da realidade, os cálculos e números de natureza estatística avançados pelo Denunciante.

 

# Concretamente, o vencedor em causa atingiu o número médio de 35 viagens por dia e 338 viagens na quarta semana da Campanha.

 

# Este atingiu o pódio porque aceitou praticamente todas as viagens solicitadas pelos passageiros, maioritariamente viagens de curta distância..

 

# Ora, numa Campanha que promove o número de viagens realizadas, a vontade em aceitar e realizar viagens coloca-o na linha da frente para subir ao pódio.

 

# Acrescente-se que nessa semana o específico motorista guiou cerca de 60 horas num período de 7 dias, plenamente em linha com os limites previstos no artigo 13.º RJTVDE.

 

# Paralelamente não podemos deixar de mencionar que, por múltiplas razões, apenas uma “unidade microscópica” dos motoristas atinge números que capacitam a subida ao pódio de uma Campanha desta natureza, pelo que desta Campanha não poderão ser desenhados padrões de atividade aplicáveis à globalidade dos motoristas que recorre à plataforma Bolt.

 

 

Certo de que os fundamentos e justificações aqui inscritos não mais conduzirão de que a um arquivamento desta Denúncia, ficamos ao dispor para qualquer informação adicional.

* +*Portaria n.º 135/2012, de 08 de Maio*+ establishes the statutes of the Social Security in PT:[https://www.pgdlisboa.pt/leis/lei_mostra_articulado.php?nid=2033&tabela=leis&so_miolo=|https://www.pgdlisboa.pt/leis/lei_mostra_articulado.php?nid=2033&tabela=leis&so_miolo=|smart-link]. +*Article 8*+ of this regulation determines that the Social Security through its Inspection department has the right to carry the necessary actions to investigation unlawful behaviour (please see below the full article)

_Article 8_
_Inspection Department_
_1 - The Supervision Department, abbreviated to DF, is responsible for supervising the fulfilment of the rights and obligations of beneficiaries and taxpayers of the social security system, private social solidarity institutions (IPSS) and other private entities that carry out social support activities._

[*Code of Criminal Procedure*|https://gddc.ministeriopublico.pt/sites/default/files/documentos/pdf/code_of_criminal_procedure_english.pdf]


* Article 132(1) – Rights and duties of witnesses – witnesses are required to present themselves to the authority by whom they have been legitimately summoned or notified, to take an oath when heard by a judicial authority, to obey any instructions legitimately given to them regarding how to give evidence and to answer questions put to them truthfully. NOTE: According to Article 132 (2), witnesses are not obliged to answer questions when they claim that their answers will result in them being held criminally responsible.
* Title III of the Criminal Procedure Code - This title includes several provisions on means of obtaining evidence, namely examination of traces of the crime and on the circumstances it was committed on persons, places, animals and things (articles 171 to 173), searches to people or locations (articles 174 to 177 and article 251) and seizures (articles 178 to 186), including seizures of any type of correspondence (articles 179 and 252).



[*Law no 109/2009, of September 15th (Cybercrime Law)*|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/lei/109-2009-489693]


* Article 14(1) - duty to communicate specific and determined computer data stored in a given computer system by whoever has availability or control of that data, if ordered by the competent judicial authority in the course of a proceeding. This also may apply to service providers which may have to provide their customer’s/client’s data, including traffic data (article 14(4)).
* Articles 16 and 17 - instances in which data may be seized when the authorities have had legitimate access to an informatic system.



[*Decree Law n.er 114/94, of May 3rd (Road Traffic Law)*|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/decreto-lei/114-1994-250659]


* Article 85(1) - obligation of the driver to carry specific documents whenever a motor vehicle is on the public highway (ID, driving license, insurance certificate, tax identification document).
* Article 89(1) and (2) - obligation to provide information whenever an accident occurs to the other parties involved and, if the accident results in death or injury, to law enforcement agents.



[*Decree-Law n.er 15/93, of January 22nd (Combat Drugs Law)*|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/legislacao-consolidada/decreto-lei/1993-58872437]


* Article 60 - duty to provide information and documents concerning assets, deposits or any other valuables belonging to individuals suspected of committing or accused of committing the crimes set out in articles 21 to 23, 25 and 28 (which include crimes of drug trafficking and organised crime) that may be requested with a view to their seizure and confiscation for the state.



[*Code of Civil Procedure*|http://bdjur.almedina.net/citem.php?field=item_id&value=1801090]


* Article 417 - Duty to cooperate in discovering the truth in conjunction with Article 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.



[*Decree-Law No. 137/2019, of September 13 (Organizational structure of the Judicial Police)*|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/legislacao-consolidada/decreto-lei/2019-124670263]


* Article 12 - Duty of cooperation.

Hi all, Klára is off this week but I can answer this. 

Klára is correct - we cannot link one FAQ article to another. This was advised by the Tools & Workflows team who manage the Support flows in the app. Basically, if you open a link to another article from within the app, it opens in a browser rather than in-app, and this is what “breaks the UI”.

Drivers can access the _Feature access requirements_ article in the same way they’d find the main SR article; browse the FAQs in the app > go to _Using Bolt app_ (same section as the “How to handle scheduled rides” article) > Open the article. Or, if they’re using the website, there is a search bar if they want to find something specific. 

We would actually like to have a “recommended articles” option instead of linking articles with hyperlinks, as this can dilute the user’s focus if they click on a link to another article (e.g., they don’t fully read the content of the first one before clicking on the link, and they may miss a key point in the article). However, this requires development and has not been a priority for the Product team. 

The content on the website and in the driver app is from the same source in GitHub, so we can’t add it just for the website, unfortunately.

_„Szanowni Panstwo,_

 

_W pierwszej kolejnosci prosze o wybaczenie za przeslanie tego e-maila na trzy powyzsze adresy - nie jestem pewny, ktory adres jest najbardziej adekwatny do mojej sprawy._

 

_Dnia 27-07-24 podrozowalem liniami Wizzair lotem numer W6 1308 z Londynu Luton na Warszawa Okecie. W zwiazku z opoznieniem ladowanie w Warszawie nastapilo po polnocy. Po wyjsciu z hali przylotow na zewnatrz, podszedlem na stanowisko postoju taksowek - i tu zaznaczam - znajdujace sie najblizej, dokladnie naprzeciwko wyjscia. Bylo to jak zauwazylem stanowisko przewozow Bolt, niemniej stwierdzilem, ze skoro maja swoje stanowisko tuz przy wyjsciu z terminala, to musza to byc bezpieczni i zweryfikowani przewoznicy. Pan do ktorego podszedlem nie potrafil powiedziec slowa po polsku ani po angielsku co wzbudzilo moje pierwsze podejrzenie, ze cos moze byc nie tak. Po pierwszym pytaniu jakie mi zadal zrozumialem, ze pytal czy bede placic gotowka czy karta, na co ja odparlem, ze to zalezy ile przejazd wyniesie. On mi odpowiedzial, ze on przyjmuje tylko gotowke, ale ze mozemy zatrzymac sie przy bankomacie i wyplacic jak cos. Nastepnie przeszlismy do adresu - podalem "skrzyzowanie rosola i plaskowickiej" (jednej z najwazniejszych arterii Ursynowa), co jednak nic nie powiedzialo panu kierowcy, gdyz on potrzebowal do swojej nawigacji w telefonie konkretnego adresu. To byla kolejna czerwona lampka dla mnie. Jak podalem dokladny adres, to pan wyspiewal mi kwote 100 zlotych za przejazd._

 

_I teraz - bedac mniej lub bardziej regularnym uzytkownikiem taksowek i znajac Warszawe, od razu wiedzialem, ze to jest duzo za duzo, nawet za taryfe nocna i zwlaszcza za przejazd nieoficjalna taksowka, a przejazdem osob z aplikacji. Podziekowalem wiec, na co Pan zaczal cos za mna wolac (nie rozumialem co mowi, najpewniej probowal negocjowac cene)._

 

_Poszedlem kawalek dalej (podkreslam - musialem przejsc kilkanascie metrow od wyjscia z terminala przylotow) by trafic na juz licencjowana, oficjalna taksowke. Tam kierowca bez problemu skojarzyl skrzyzowanie docelowe i przejazd wyniosl mnie 64 zlote._

 

_Cala ta historia by mnie nie bulwersowala gdybym tego pana od Bolta spotkal gdzies na miescie na ulicy - kretacze sie zdarzaja. Ale w glowie mi sie nie miesci, ze tuz przy wyjsciu z najwazniejszego lotniska naszej stolicy, na najbardziej prestizowych stanowiskach postojowych nie czekaja licencjonowani taksowkarze, a naciagacze z aplikacji (w tej sytuacji Bolta). Jestem w pelni swiadom, ze Panstwo zdajecie sobie sprawe, ze przez Wasze lotnisko podrozuja osoby, ktore Warszawy nie znaja i ktore sa narazone na wykorzystanie przez takich kretaczy._

 

_Chcialbym tym e-mailem zaapelowac o zapewnienie podroznym bezpiecznych przejazdow i przewoznikow, ktorzy sa licencjonowani. W drugiej kolejnosci, gdzies w odleglosci moga miec swoje miejsca inni przewoznicy (wszak przez aplikacje i tak klient z kierowca sie znajda).”_

*Summary:*

Revolut acts:

* as a data controller - where it providers services to its customers directly.
* as a data processor - where it providers services to Bolt and facilitates payment between Bolt and Bolt`s customers.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Where Revolut acts as a data controller:*

* it undertakes to comply with its own obligations under the privacy law
* process data for a limited set of its own purposes (outlined in the DPA)
* includes clauses that very generally clarify the terms of collaboration between Revolut and Bolt as data controllers in cases of: DSRs, data breaches, and demonstrating compliance.

Overall, no red flags for the part where Revolut acts as a data controller - GDPR compliance is ensued, and Revolut undertakes to be liable for its activities as a data controller :green_square: . 

*However, the collaboration clauses do not provide the same clarity as Bolt`s standard agreement for data controller - these can be optionally clarified by attaching our template.*
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*Where Revolut acts as a data processor:*

The compliance with the GDPR is ensured - no red flags identified:green_square: :

* obligations and rights of the controller and the processor under Art. 28 requirements included
* list of sub-processors attached
* list of security measures under Art. 32 attached
* description of transfer clarified (subject-matter, duration, nature, purpose, categories of personal data and data subjects).

However, the DPA does not comply with Bolt internal standard for data processors. 

*Most important points to be improved* :red_square: *:*

# notification of DSRs - timelines not clarified. Bolt`s standard: 3 business days notice at least.
# Liability - limitation to the value of twelve (12) months of the Fees (200 k EUR). Bolt`s standard: at max, the fallback position is 1 million euros cap per claim.
# Limitation of audit rights: permitted to conduct once per 12 months; Bolt`s standard: audits can be conducted at reasonable time intervals or if there is a suspicion of non-compliance by the processor;
# notification of data breaches - timelines not clarified (undue delay). Bolt`s standard: 48 h notice at least.
# Custom information security standards, outlined in Appendix 3 - we need to add a clause clarifying that Revolut confirms that the measures must always comply with Bolt`s security standard. 
# Use of sub-processors - 14 days authorisation notice. Bolt`s standard: at least 20 days authorisation notice.
# Revolut will charge reasonable costs for the assistance provided to Bolt under Art. 32-36 (DPIAs assistance, consultations with DPAs). Bolt`s standard: this can be acceptable provided that assistance goes above and beyond what would reasonably be expected during the ordinary course of business and prior notice is issued.
# Audits are fully at the cost of Bolt. Per Bolt's standards: costs can be shared, provided that if there is a negative audit finding, the Processor shall be responsible for the cost.

Points that add little legal risk but differentiate from Bolt`s standards :yellow_square: :

# Use of sub-processors - general authorisation. Bolt`s standard: specific authorisation, but exceptions can be made for trusted and audited processors.
# Limitation of audit rights: 30 days prior notice. Per Bolt's standards: two weeks notice.
# Onward International Data Transfers: permitted by default provided that the lawfulness of the transfer is ensured. Bolt`s standard: processor must seek specific authorisation.
{panel}

*Advice intention:*

* to push back on the provisions marked as :red_square:  (1-8), which add the most legal risks.
* considering the provider is in Lithuania, the size of the provider, and overall good reputation (no GDPR fines issued) - provisions marked :yellow_square: (9-11) can be left as is due to low impact.

** UPDATED THOUGHTS BASED ON INPUT **

{color:#403294}*SUMMARY*{color}:

* Sending this email / the form to drivers does not appear to raise any obvious issues from a privacy perspective (subject to [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e]'s and [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425]'s thoughts).
* The main issue with the proposed activity is the _data we would be processing to calculate whether a driver has one the competition_ - in particular, safety cases and interactions with CS, which seems intrusive.
* It seems we have three options:
** (a) Tell Karolina that although this is a good idea in principle, processing driver’s safety / CS information is too intrusive just for the sake of a promotional competition, and on balance we should not proceed with this.
** (b) Proceed with the proposed processing activities, but ensure that robust transparency wording is included in the form and we have a clear legal basis for the proposed processing activities.
** (c) See if there is any wiggle room for measuring any of the three conditions in less intrusive ways, and then proceeding on that basis.

[~accountid:63622ea17d4645af4f03bd18] - what are your views on these options? They are fleshed out in full below, together with the reasoning.

----

{color:#403294}*ANALYSIS*{color}:

*(1) Sending the email to drivers asking them to take part in the competition*

* It would be best to just email drivers (rather than also call them) from a data minimisation perspective.
* Our legal basis for sending these emails out to the drivers in the first place would be {color:#4c9aff}*legitimate interest*{color} (i.e., legitimate interest in promoting our services and conducting sweepstakes to deepen our existing relationship with our drivers / develop new ones).
* [~accountid:712020:b2a2738f-c1f1-447c-9b72-29851b5fed3e] - as mentioned below, would you be able to advise on whether this raises any risks from a direct marketing perspective (given there is a promotional element here)? I assume not, but just to be sure.
* [~accountid:62722e092db308007024a425] - just wanted to loop you in on this briefly as well. In short, per the ticket description, Bolt wants to invite Lithuanian drivers to compete in a competition to either: (a) complete the most rides in August; (b) get the best driver score; or (c) invite the most friends to the platform. I know that reclass risk is more of an issue in the UK, but from your perspective, does this present any obvious issues as it could be seen as ‘Bolt encouraging drivers to drive more’ etc.?

*(2) Collecting the driver’s name and email in the form*

* This is low risk, not excessive, and for a relatively clear purpose.
* The applicable legal basis here should be {color:#4c9aff}*consent*{color} - drivers are opting-in to the competition, and so should be opting-in to their personal data being used in this context. The Ops team should ensure there is a process in place for if a driver subsequently withdraws their consent.
* The main issue to address here is {color:#ff5630}*transparency*{color} - the current driver privacy notice does not cover this processing activity. As such, we should revise the wording in the form to include some transparency wording (and to explicitly address the collection of consent) - see draft wording below at (4). We can then ensure that the master driver privacy notice is updated to include this type of processing.

*(3) Processing the driver’s data about completed trips / driver rating / number of friends invited to the platform*

* Based on Karolina’s responses, once a driver as confirmed they will participate in the competition, Bolt will use the following to measure whether they have succeeded in any of the three conditions:
** +Most completed trips+: We will process: (1) the number of completed rides (which makes sense); and (2) information on any safety / quality cases and interactions with CS (this is {color:#ff5630}*more high risk*{color} - it will contain more sensitive information and the driver is unlikely to expect this). My thinking is the latter is likely to be intrusive.
** +Best driver rating+: We will process: (1) the driver’s average / best rating (again, which makes sense); and (2) the same safety / quality / CS information as above (again, this is {color:#ff5630}*more high risk*{color}). My thinking is the latter is likely to be intrusive.
** +Most friends invited to Bolt+: This involves only processing the number of ‘codes’ of the driver that have been used. This seems ok.
* Bolt appears to be processing this data already, and so the processing is not new. However, as this appears to be the first time we have run a competition like this, it is processing this data for a {color:#4c9aff}*new purpose*{color} (i.e., measuring eligibility to win the competition). As such, we need to consider legal basis and transparency issues here.
** +Legal basis+: We could consider {color:#4c9aff}*consent*{color} as a legal basis here, given that only drivers that opt-in to the competition should have their data processed for this purpose. However, this is {color:#ff5630}*risky*{color}, and we would need to be super-specific in our transparency wording on what exactly the driver is consenting to - I doubt that all drivers would be fine with the safety data / CS interactions being reviewed just for the sake of a competition. [~accountid:63622ea17d4645af4f03bd18] - what are your views on this?
** +Transparency+: We can address this in the same way as proposed above (see the draft wording at (4)).

*(4) Options*

* *Option 1* - Tell Karolina not to proceed with this.
** As summarised above, my main concern here is that the metrics we would be using to determine if a driver has won may be quite intrusive in a few cases, particularly with regards to safety / CS data. Processing these data categories may not be worth the risk, given that this is just intended as a nice competition.
* *Option 2* - Give this the green light, provided we implement robust consent / transparency wording.
** Technically, the processing activities proposed to measure whether a driver has won may be fine if we have a proper legal basis in place and appropriate transparency wording.  We could consider addressing these concerns by including the following wording:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
“_By submitting this form, you confirm we can use your name and e-mail to determine and announce the_ _competition winner._ _You also confirm that we can use the following data that we have about you to measure whether you are successful in this competition:_

* _Your number of completed trips_
* _Your driver rating_
* _Information on any previous safety and/or quality cases in which you have been involved, and data concerning previous interactions with Bolt Customer Support_
* _Number of your driver codes used by other individuals when signing up to Bolt_

_We conduct this survey and campaign based on our legitimate interest in learning more about your awareness as drivers of specific safety features. For more information on how we process your data, your rights, and our contact details, please see the Privacy Notice for Drivers_: [LINK]”
{panel}

* *Option 3* - Explore less intrusive methods of measuring the three conditions, and then strategise accordingly.
** I will shortly send Karolina a message double-checking whether there are any other options for measuring the three conditions here, as this is the main blocker from my perspective. However, she may come back and say that the proposed approach is the only one we can take.

[~accountid:63622ea17d4645af4f03bd18] - what are your thoughts on approach here, in light of he above?

[~accountid:63cfbe91c565900ff404f491] - as I review, one immediate thought is that reviewing a driver’s +previous safety / quality cases+ and +the way they interact with CS+ seems quite intrusive and may complicate things from a privacy perspective - *are there any alternatives to processing this information about drivers that would still achieve the intended result* (i.e., measuring the number of a driver’s rides and their rating?)/

If the order indicated that the driver was not moving then not to compensate the CF is a correct solution. 

_A cancellation fee is the compensation that is automatically added to your earnings when:_

* The rider cancels after a certain time frame of you accepting their order and *driving towards their pickup location*.

*Depo (Elīna L) comments:*

Agreeing to the T&C and entering into/executing a contract are two different things. From the point of view of processing personal data, Bolt and the company are the contracting parties, and the company transfers the personal data of the users (employees). It is not a natural person who concludes the contract and submits their personal data, but the company. Therefore, the processing cannot be based on the conclusion and performance of the contract.

To be justified under Article 6(1)(b) of the GDPR, the contract has to be concluded with each user (employee) separately. In this situation, I see Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR - legitimate interest - as the legal basis, for example, to identify users and see the amounts spent on Bolt services by each user.
{panel}

*Response:*

This is correct. We cannot rely on the lawful basis of under Article 6(1)(b) of the GDPR (Bolt Business T&C) to process the personal data of users. We confirm that Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR - legitimate interest - is the lawful basis to process personal data in this context.

This is clarified in the last update of our privacy notices ([https://bolt.eu/lv-lv/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/lv-lv/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|smart-link] ), quote:

It is correct that two processes:

Dear Iboro Umoh

 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *16 July 2024.* 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Trip history from February 2024- July 2034* 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,



Bolt
